claims.text: The extent and uniformity of surface oxidation during friction are the dominant factors governing the wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
A moderate, uniformly distributed oxide film acts as an in situ lubricious layer that reduces metal-to-metal contact and wear.
Excessive or non-uniform oxidation produces brittle, fragmented oxide debris.
Fragmented oxide debris increases abrasive and adhesive wear.
The proposed initial coating is an as-deposited, homogeneous AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy.
Changing oxygen partial pressure or temperature during wear testing will control the oxidation level.
The controlled comparison will be conducted at 800–900 °C while load, speed, and contact geometry are held constant.
Wear produces surface oxide phases such as Al2O3 and Cr2O3 whose thickness and uniformity mediate performance.
Under moderate oxidative conditions, a thin, continuous oxide layer reduces direct metal contact and frictional energy dissipation.
Excessive oxidation produces thick or uneven scales that crack or spall and expose fresh substrate.
Reducing oxygen concentration relative to air will produce a moderate, uniform oxide film.
Reducing oxygen concentration relative to air will lower the coating wear rate.
Higher oxygen exposure will produce non-uniform oxide layers and increase wear through abrasion and adhesion.
Wear testing in standard air at 800–900 °C is likely to cause excessive, non-uniform oxidation and mixed wear mechanisms.
The hypothesis applies to high-temperature wear environments such as hot-end components and steam pipelines.
The hypothesis may not apply at low or room temperature because oxidation kinetics are significantly slower.
The threshold separating beneficial and detrimental oxidation depends on alloy composition and wear parameters.
SEM and EDS characterization, together with mass-loss or profilometry measurements, can test the proposed oxide-film and wear-rate relationship.

contradictions.description: The mechanism requires a moderate oxide film for low wear, but the proposed low-oxygen condition includes near-zero oxygen and is nevertheless predicted to form that beneficial film. Near-zero oxygen could instead suppress oxide formation, so reduced oxygen is not consistently distinguished from moderate oxidation.
